summary.text: Natural selection means that individuals with different traits survive and reproduce at different rates.
It is a key mechanism of evolution, changing the heritable traits of a population or species over generations.
Because some traits make survival and reproductive success more likely, those traits are more likely to be passed on to the next generation.

items.prompt: A farmer picks only the sweetest plants to breed each year. How does that differ from what happens in the wild?

options.label: The farmer changes traits, while nature can never change them
The farmer chooses on purpose, while nature has no intention
The farmer's choice cannot be inherited, while nature's can
There is no difference, as both are equally intentional

items.explain: Artificial selection is intentional, whereas natural selection is not.

items.prompt: Suppose every individual in a population were exactly alike in every trait that gets passed down. What would selection have to act on?

options.label: The strongest individuals, who would still be chosen
Only the environment, which would pick winners itself
Whichever traits happen to be the newest ones
Nothing; it needs inherited differences to act on

items.explain: Selection of the most advantageous variations needs some variation between individuals, and that variation must be heritable.

items.prompt: A trait helps its owners survive and have young, and their surroundings stay the same for many generations. What can happen to the trait?

options.label: It can become more common in the population
It disappears, because nothing is changing
It becomes rarer, since stable surroundings punish it
It stays exactly as common, whatever its benefit

items.explain: Traits that favour survival and reproduction can become more common within a population if the environment that favours them remains fixed.

items.prompt: A climate shift across a whole region changes which traits are favoured everywhere, not just inside one habitat niche. Which term fits?

options.label: Microevolution
Artificial selection
Macroevolution
Fecundity selection

items.explain: New traits becoming favoured through changes in the broader environment is called macroevolution, while changes in a specific niche give microevolution.

items.prompt: Under Lamarck's early 19th-century idea, what would a blacksmith's children get from his years of building strong arms?

options.label: They could inherit nothing, as acquired traits never pass on
They could inherit the strength he gained during life
They could inherit it only through their mother's genes
They could inherit it only if they also became blacksmiths

items.explain: Lamarck suggested that adaptive traits acquired during an organism's lifetime could be inherited by its offspring.

items.prompt: A river's small daily erosion carves a canyon over vast ages. Why did geology's success with this idea make natural selection easier to accept?

options.label: Tiny changes over generations could add up to differences between species
It proved that species never change, however long the time
It showed that weak forces cannot act over long periods of time
It proved that only sudden disasters can reshape living things

items.explain: Uniformitarianism raised awareness of the vast scale of geological time and made plausible that tiny changes in successive generations could produce differences between species.

paragraphs.heading: Who survives and breeds
paragraphs.text: Natural selection is the way individuals with different traits survive and reproduce at different rates. What decides the outcome is their relative fitness, which comes from the particular set of observable traits each one has. Over generations, this process changes the inherited traits typical of a population or a species. It is a key mechanism of evolution.

paragraphs.heading: How it works
paragraphs.text: Every population contains variation, both in genes and in visible traits. Some traits make it more likely that an individual will survive and have offspring, so those traits are more likely to reach the next generation. If the environment that favours them stays the same, they can become more common across the population. Darwin summed it up as the principle by which each small variation, if useful, is kept.

paragraphs.heading: An inevitable result
paragraphs.text: The core idea is simple. Individuals that suit their surroundings best tend to survive and reproduce more. So long as individuals differ and those differences can be inherited, the ones with the most helpful variations will be selected without fail. Natural selection is still the main explanation for adaptive evolution, even though genotypes can also drift slowly by chance.

paragraphs.heading: Other kinds of selection
paragraphs.text: Many factors decide whether a trait gets passed on. Some traits spread because they help their owners cope with the environment. Others spread because mates actively prefer them, which is called sexual selection. Darwin set natural selection beside artificial selection, in which human breeders deliberately favour plants and animals with traits they want; natural selection, by contrast, has no intention behind it.

paragraphs.heading: Ideas before Darwin
paragraphs.text: Hints of the idea appeared long before. As the 16th century began, Leonardo da Vinci reasoned that animal shapes are not fixed once and for all, but arise naturally in various forms and are then selected by how well they fit their surroundings. Geology also helped. Uniformitarianism held that weak forces working steadily over long ages could reshape a landscape, and its success made it believable that tiny changes from one generation to the next could add up to differences between species.

paragraphs.heading: Darwin and Wallace
paragraphs.text: Charles Darwin and Alfred Russel Wallace presented the concept together in papers read in 1858. Darwin expanded it the next year in On the Origin of Species, offering it as an explanation for both adaptation and the origin of new species. At the time, science had no sound theory of heredity. Joining Darwin's ideas with later discoveries in genetics produced the modern synthesis in the mid-20th century.

paragraphs.heading: Small and large change
paragraphs.text: When new traits gain an advantage because a particular niche changes, the result is microevolution. When they gain an advantage because the wider environment changes, the result is macroevolution. New species can sometimes arise, especially when the new traits differ sharply from those of their ancestors.
